title: Algebraic Expressions
summary: Classify real numbers, convert recurring decimals to fractions, round off and estimate surds, and multiply out algebraic expressions including binomial-by-trinomial products.

notes.text: The real number system

Every number you use in Grade 10 belongs to one or more **sets** (groups) of numbers. Knowing which set a number belongs to helps you understand what you can and cannot do with it. The sets fit inside each other, a bit like a learner who is part of a class, which is part of a grade, which is part of a school.
The counting numbers: $\mathbb{N} = \{1;\ 2;\ 3;\ 4;\ \ldots\}$.
The natural numbers together with zero: $\mathbb{N}_0 = \{0;\ 1;\ 2;\ 3;\ \ldots\}$.
The whole numbers and their negatives: $\mathbb{Z} = \{\ldots;\ -3;\ -2;\ -1;\ 0;\ 1;\ 2;\ 3;\ \ldots\}$.

Any number that can be written as a fraction $\dfrac{a}{b}$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers and $b \neq 0$. As decimals, rational numbers either **terminate** (end), e.g. $0{,}75$, or **recur** (repeat a pattern forever), e.g. $0{,}333\ldots$. Every integer is rational, because, for example, $-4 = \dfrac{-4}{1}$.

Numbers that **cannot** be written as a fraction of two integers. Their decimals go on forever **without** a repeating pattern. Examples: $\pi = 3{,}14159\ldots$, $\sqrt{2} = 1{,}41421\ldots$, $\sqrt{7}$ and $\sqrt[3]{5}$.
All the rational and irrational numbers together. Every real number has a place on the number line.

Numbers that are not on the real number line, such as the square root of a negative number, e.g. $\sqrt{-4}$. No real number multiplied by itself gives $-4$, because a positive times a positive and a negative times a negative are both positive. You only need to recognise the term in Grade 10.

Classifying numbers (✓ = belongs to the set)

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: $\dfrac{22}{7}$ is **rational** (it is a fraction of integers), but $\pi$ is **irrational**. $\dfrac{22}{7}$ is only an approximation of $\pi$. Also, a square root is not automatically irrational: $\sqrt{9} = 3$ and $\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$ are rational. Remember too that division by zero is **undefined**, so $\dfrac{5}{0}$ is not a number at all.
Converting recurring decimals to common fractions

A **recurring decimal** repeats a digit or a block of digits forever. We show this with dots above the repeating digits: $0{,}\dot{3}$ means $0{,}333\ldots$ and $0{,}\dot{1}\dot{2}$ means $0{,}121212\ldots$ (the dots go above the **first** and **last** digit of the repeating block). Some books use a bar instead: $0{,}\overline{12}$.

Because recurring decimals are rational, we can always write them as a fraction. The trick is to multiply so that the repeating parts line up, and then subtract to make them disappear.

items: Let $x$ equal the recurring decimal. Write out a few repeats.
Multiply by $10$ if **one** digit repeats, by $100$ if **two** digits repeat, by $1\,000$ if **three** digits repeat.
Subtract the original equation so that the repeating tails cancel.
Solve for $x$ and simplify the fraction.

notes.title: Worked example 1: one repeating digit
steps: One digit repeats, so multiply by $10$: $10x = 3{,}333\ldots$ ... (2)

notes.title: Worked example 2: two repeating digits
notes.problem: Write $0{,}\dot{1}\dot{2}$ as a common fraction in simplest form.
steps: Two digits repeat, so multiply by $100$: $100x = 12{,}121212\ldots$ ... (2)

notes.title: Worked example 3: a digit before the repeating part
notes.problem: Write $0{,}1\dot{6}$ (that is, $0{,}1666\ldots$) as a common fraction.
steps: Move the decimal comma past the non-repeating digit: $10x = 1{,}666\ldots$ ... (1)
Move it one more place (one repeating digit): $100x = 16{,}666\ldots$ ... (2)

notes.title: Worked example 4: a number greater than 1

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: You must show the algebraic method (let $x = \ldots$, multiply, subtract). Writing only the answer from a calculator earns very few marks. Check your answer by dividing on a calculator: $27 \div 11 = 2{,}454545\ldots$ ✓
Rounding off real numbers

Irrational numbers and long decimals are often **rounded off** to a given number of decimal places. Look only at the digit **immediately after** the last digit you want to keep:

• If it is $5$ or more ($5;\ 6;\ 7;\ 8;\ 9$), round **up** (add $1$ to the last kept digit).
• If it is less than $5$ ($0;\ 1;\ 2;\ 3;\ 4$), round **down** (leave the last kept digit as it is).

Then drop all the digits after the last kept one.

notes.title: Worked example 5: rounding
notes.problem: Round off (a) $\pi = 3{,}14159\ldots$ to two and to three decimal places, (b) $12{,}6973$ to two decimal places, (c) $0{,}04449$ to three decimal places.
steps: (a) Two decimal places: keep $3{,}14$; the next digit is $1$ (less than $5$), so $\pi \approx 3{,}14$. Three decimal places: keep $3{,}141$; the next digit is $5$, so round up: $\pi \approx 3{,}142$.
(b) Keep $12{,}69$; the next digit is $7$, so round up. $69$ hundredths becomes $70$ hundredths: $12{,}70$. Keep the final zero, because the question asks for two decimal places.
(c) Keep $0{,}044$; the next digit is $4$, so round down: $0{,}044$.

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Do not round in stages. Rounding $0{,}04449$ first to $0{,}0445$ and then to $0{,}045$ is **wrong**; only the digit straight after the required place counts. Also, in a long calculation keep all the digits in your calculator and round **only the final answer**.
Estimating surds

A **surd** is a root that cannot be simplified to a rational number, such as $\sqrt{30}$ or $\sqrt[3]{50}$. Without a calculator you can still say which two **consecutive integers** (whole numbers next to each other) a surd lies between. To do this you need to know your perfect squares and perfect cubes.

notes.caption: Perfect squares and cubes worth knowing

notes.title: Worked example 6: square roots
notes.problem: Between which two consecutive integers does $\sqrt{30}$ lie?
steps: Find the perfect squares on either side of $30$: $25 < 30 < 36$.
Take the square root of each part: $\sqrt{25} < \sqrt{30} < \sqrt{36}$.
So $5 < \sqrt{30} < 6$. Since $30$ is much closer to $25$ than to $36$, $\sqrt{30}$ is closer to $5$ (a calculator gives $5{,}477\ldots$).

notes.title: Worked example 7: cube roots and negative surds
notes.problem: Between which two consecutive integers do (a) $\sqrt[3]{50}$ and (b) $-\sqrt{45}$ lie?
steps: Multiplying by $-1$ reverses the inequality signs: $-7 < -\sqrt{45} < -6$.

notes.text: Algebraic language
Before multiplying expressions, make sure you know the vocabulary. In the expression $3x^2 - 5xy + 7$:

items: **Terms** are separated by $+$ and $-$ signs: $3x^2$, $-5xy$ and $7$.
The **coefficient** is the number in front of the variable(s): the coefficient of $x^2$ is $3$ and the coefficient of $xy$ is $-5$.
A **constant** is a term with no variable: $7$.
**Like terms** have exactly the same variables with the same exponents, e.g. $4a^2b$ and $-9a^2b$. $x^2$ and $x^3$ are **not** like terms.
A **monomial** has one term ($-6p^3$), a **binomial** has two terms ($2x + 5$) and a **trinomial** has three terms ($x^2 + 4x - 1$).

notes.text: To **add or subtract**, collect only like terms: add or subtract the coefficients and keep the variable part the same.

notes.title: Worked example 8: like terms and monomials
steps: (b) Multiply the coefficients and add the exponents of each variable: $(-2)(5)\,x^{2+1}\,y^{1+3} = -10x^3y^4$.
(c) Use the **distributive law** $a(b + c) = ab + ac$: $(-3a)(2a) + (-3a)(-5b) = -6a^2 + 15ab$.

notes.text: Multiplying two binomials
Each term in the first bracket multiplies each term in the second bracket. A useful memory aid is **FOIL**: **F**irst, **O**uter, **I**nner, **L**ast. Then collect like terms.

notes.title: Worked example 9
steps: F: $2x \times x = 2x^2$;  O: $2x \times (-4) = -8x$;  I: $3 \times x = 3x$;  L: $3 \times (-4) = -12$

notes.text: **Squaring a binomial** means multiplying it by itself. Two patterns come up so often that you should know them by heart:

notes.caption: Sum times difference: the middle terms cancel

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: $(a + b)^2 \neq a^2 + b^2$. Test it with numbers: $(3 + 4)^2 = 49$, but $3^2 + 4^2 = 25$. The missing $2ab = 24$ is the middle term.
Multiplying a binomial by a trinomial

The method is the same: multiply **each** term of the binomial by **every** term of the trinomial. That gives $2 \times 3 = 6$ products. Write them in order of descending powers, then collect like terms. Working in two lines (one line for each term of the binomial) keeps you organised.

notes.title: Worked example 11
steps: Add and collect like terms: $3x^3 + (-6x^2 - x^2) + (15x + 2x) - 5$

notes.text: Two special products: sum and difference of cubes
When a binomial is multiplied by a particular trinomial, all the middle terms cancel and only two cubes are left. These products are the starting point for factorising cubes in the next topic.

notes.title: Worked example 12
steps: The $x^2$ terms cancel and the $x$ terms cancel: $x^3 + 8$. (This matches $a^3 + b^3$ with $a = x$, $b = 2$.)

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Look at the trinomial: its middle term is the **opposite sign** of the binomial's sign, and its last term is the **square** of the binomial's second term. If you spot $(x - 5)(x^2 + 5x + 25)$ you can write $x^3 - 125$ straight away, but show at least one line of working in a test.
Simplifying longer expressions

Many exam questions combine several products. Expand each part separately inside brackets, then remove the brackets carefully. A minus sign in front of a bracket changes the sign of **every** term inside.

notes.title: Worked example 13
steps: Remove the brackets; the minus changes both signs: $x^2 - 4x + 4 - x^2 + 9$

notes.label: Common mistake
notes.text: Writing $(x - 2)^2 - (x + 3)(x - 3) = x^2 - 4x + 4 - x^2 - 9$ is wrong. The $-9$ inside the second bracket becomes $+9$ when the bracket is subtracted.
Summary

items: $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{N}_0 \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$; irrational numbers ($\mathbb{Q}'$) are real but not rational. Square roots of negative numbers are non-real.
Rational numbers can be written as $\frac{a}{b}$ ($a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$, $b \neq 0$); their decimals terminate or recur. Irrational decimals never end and never repeat.
To convert a recurring decimal: let $x = $ the decimal, multiply by $10$, $100$ or $1\,000$, subtract to cancel the repeating tail, solve and simplify.
To round off, look at the next digit only: $5$ or more rounds up, less than $5$ rounds down. Round only the final answer.
Estimate a surd using the perfect squares (or cubes) on either side of it, e.g. $5 < \sqrt{30} < 6$.
Collect only like terms. Multiply each term of one bracket by every term of the other.
A minus sign in front of a bracket changes the sign of every term inside it.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following numbers is **irrational**?
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{16} = 4$, $0{,}\dot{7} = \frac{7}{9}$ and $\frac{22}{7}$ are all fractions of integers, so they are rational. $7$ is not a perfect square, so $\sqrt{7} = 2{,}6457\ldots$ never ends or repeats.

questions.prompt: To which one of these sets does $-5$ belong?
questions.explanation: Natural and whole numbers are never negative. $-5 = \frac{-5}{1}$ is rational, not irrational. It is an integer.
No real number squared gives a negative answer: $3^2 = 9$ and $(-3)^2 = 9$. So $\sqrt{-9}$ is non-real.

questions.prompt: $0{,}\dot{1}\dot{2}$ is irrational because its decimal digits never end.
questions.explanation: The digits never end, but they **repeat**, so the number is rational: $0{,}\dot{1}\dot{2} = \frac{12}{99} = \frac{4}{33}$. Irrational decimals never end **and** never repeat.

questions.prompt: Match each number with the description that fits it best.

pairs.right: Whole number, but not a natural number
Integer, but not a whole number

questions.explanation: $0$ is in $\mathbb{N}_0$ but not $\mathbb{N}$; $-\sqrt{25} = -5$ is an integer; $\frac{3}{8} = 0{,}375$ terminates so it is rational; $\pi$ never ends or repeats; the square root of a negative number is non-real.

questions.prompt: Round off $7{,}4865$ correct to **two** decimal places.
questions.explanation: Keep $7{,}48$. The next digit is $6$ ($5$ or more), so round up: $7{,}49$.

questions.prompt: Without using a calculator, between which two consecutive integers does $\sqrt{75}$ lie?
Between which two consecutive integers does $\sqrt[3]{100}$ lie?
Use an algebraic method to write $0{,}\dot{2}\dot{7}$ as a common fraction in its simplest form.
questions.memo:

questions.prompt: Sipho says that $0{,}\dot{9}$ is slightly less than $1$. Use algebra to show that $0{,}\dot{9} = 1$.
Expand and simplify $(3x - 2)(2x + 5)$. What is the coefficient of $x$ in your answer?
The product $(x + 3)(x^2 - 3x + 9)$ simplifies to $x^3 + k$. Find the value of $k$.
questions.explanation: $x^3 - 3x^2 + 9x + 3x^2 - 9x + 27 = x^3 + 27$. This is the sum of cubes $a^3 + b^3$ with $b = 3$, so $k = 3^3 = 27$.
